Pronunciation note for this grammar point:
The auxiliary is stressed when it corrects an assumption: so DOES she. Otherwise so and neither are unstressed and the subject carries the stress.

elements.content: Grammar focus: So and Neither.

Look at the statement you are agreeing with. Positive: so plus the same auxiliary plus the subject. Negative: neither plus the same auxiliary plus the subject. Keep the auxiliary and the tense, and invert the subject.

so + auxiliary + subject — positive agreement: so does she
neither + auxiliary + subject — negative agreement: neither do I
auxiliary repeats the original — be, have, do or a modal: so have we, neither can he
tense stays the same — no change of tense: she has signed — so have we
nor — formal variant of neither: nor has she
me too / me neither — informal equivalents: me too, me neither
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Complete: 'She has a car, and ___ has he.'
2. Complete: 'They didn't call, and ___ did we.'
3. Complete: 'He can swim, and so ___ she.'
Read and listen: three examples in context.

I like coffee, and so does she. — Positive, so plus the auxiliary. (So does she = she likes it too.)
I don't like tea, and neither do I. — Negative, neither plus the auxiliary. (Neither do I = I don't either.)
She can't come, and neither can he. — Modal negative. (Neither can he.)
What do you observe?

So and neither agree with the previous speaker by repeating the auxiliary and inverting the subject. A positive statement takes so: so do I, so has she, so can we. A negative statement takes neither (or nor in formal writing): neither do I, neither has she. The auxiliary must match the original verb, and the tense stays the same.
1. Which word agrees with a negative statement?
2. What follows so or neither?
State the rule in one sentence, without looking at the table.
Freer production: I can agree and disagree with so and neither.

Success criteria:
- I can agree with a positive statement using so.
- I can agree with a negative statement using neither.
- I can repeat the right auxiliary and tense.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ I like coffee, and so do I (so with the wrong subject for agreement) → ✅ I like coffee, and so does she
❌ I don't like tea, and so don't I (so used with a negative statement) → ✅ I don't like tea, and neither do I
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

We have finished, and so have they.
He won't sign, and neither will the chair.
The panel has not reported, nor has the board.
Adapt the same task to the group:

- Individual: five sentences with the structure, on the topic of the lesson.
- Pair: a ten-line dialogue where all, both, either, neither, none carries the argument.
- Group: a six-minute debate, two sides, the structure required in every turn.
- Professional audience: transpose the structure into a memo.
- Academic audience: transpose it into a paragraph of analysis.

Second grammar point of the lesson: All, Both, Either, Neither, None. Count first: two things take both, either or neither; three or more take all or none. Then match the verb: both and all plural, either and neither singular, none singular in formal
